introduction-the-vector-of-the-ship.core: Effort only adds up when it points the same way. Strategic planning aligns many people's work toward shared goals, replacing the ambient context a tiny startup gets for free.

first_principles.problem: At 10 people everyone knows the goal. At 200, teams push in different directions, and enormous total effort barely moves the company.
truths: Effort in different directions cancels out.
Context stops being ambient as companies grow.
Explicit goals scale; hallway conversations don't.
derivation: State **few, clear goals**.
Cascade them so each team knows **its contribution**.
Measure **health** (KPIs) separately from **change** (OKRs).

analogy.title: Ten people pushing a car
analogy.story: Five pushing forward and five sideways barely move it. All ten pushing forward and it rolls.
analogy.breaks: A car has one obvious direction. Companies must choose and communicate theirs.

example.title: Two teams, conflicting goals
example.scenario: Growth team adds sign-up steps; platform team cuts latency.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Both teams optimise the same activation metric.

check.q: Why do larger companies need explicit strategy?
check.a: Context is no longer shared informally, so teams drift in different directions.

kpis-the-dashboard-of-organizational-hea.core: KPIs are vital signs: measures that confirm the business, team or service is healthy (uptime, latency, revenue, deploy frequency). You watch them constantly and act only when they leave normal ranges.

first_principles.problem: Teams track dozens of metrics without knowing which matter, or confuse health monitoring with improvement goals.
derivation: Pick a **small set** of KPIs per team.
Define **healthy ranges** and alerts.
Use KPIs to **keep things running**; use OKRs to **change** things.

analogy.title: A doctor's vital signs
analogy.story: Heart rate, blood pressure and temperature are checked routinely; only abnormal readings trigger treatment.
analogy.breaks: Vital signs are standard across humans. KPIs must be chosen per team.

example.title: Platform team KPIs
example.outcome: health is visible without constant attention.

check.q: How do KPIs differ from OKRs?
check.a: KPIs monitor ongoing health; OKRs drive deliberate change.

okrs-the-engine-of-deliberate-change.core: OKRs set an inspiring qualitative Objective and 2–5 measurable Key Results that show it was achieved. They're for deliberate change, typically ambitious (70% achievement is good).

first_principles.problem: Goals like 'improve reliability' are unmeasurable, and task lists ('migrate to K8s') confuse output with outcome.
derivation: **Objective**: qualitative direction ('Make deploys boring').
**Key Results**: outcomes with numbers ('lead time < 1 h', 'change failure < 5%').
Keep **few** (3 objectives max).
Grade at quarter end; **don't tie to bonuses**.

analogy.title: A road trip destination and milestones
analogy.story: "Get to the coast" is the objective; "reach town X by noon, 400 km by evening" are key results.
analogy.breaks: Road trips end. OKRs repeat quarterly and should evolve.

example.title: Platform team OKR

steps.label: Not a KR
steps.detail: "Adopt ArgoCD" is a task, not an outcome.

example.outcome: the team knows what success looks like, not just what to do.

check.q: Is 'Migrate to Kubernetes' a good key result?
check.a: No, it's a task; a key result measures an outcome, like deploy lead time.

wartime-vs-peacetime-leadership.core: Leadership style should fit the situation. In peacetime (growth, stability) leaders empower, explore and build consensus; in wartime (existential threat, major outage) they focus, direct and cut everything non-essential.

first_principles.problem: A consensus-driven leader keeps debating during a crisis, or a command-style leader micromanages a stable team and kills initiative.
truths: Stable periods reward creativity and autonomy.
derivation: Diagnose: **is there an existential threat?**
**Wartime**: single priority, clear directives, fast decisions.
**Peacetime**: autonomy, experimentation, broad goals.
Switch **explicitly** and tell the team.

analogy.title: A ship in calm seas vs a storm
analogy.story: In calm water the crew can explore and improve. In a storm, the captain gives direct orders and everyone executes.
analogy.breaks: Storms are obvious. Business crises sometimes build slowly, so leaders must call the switch.

example.title: A security breach

steps.label: Communicate
steps.detail: Leaders say explicitly that normal process is suspended, and when it will resume.

example.outcome: the crisis gets full focus, and autonomy returns after.

check.q: What's a risk of staying in wartime mode too long?
check.a: Burnout and loss of initiative and creativity across the team.

the-quarterly-cycle.core: Quarters (12–13 weeks) are long enough for meaningful work and short enough to correct course. A cycle of plan → execute with check-ins → review and grade keeps strategy current.

first_principles.problem: Annual plans go stale within months; weekly re-planning causes thrash. Teams need a rhythm in between.
derivation: **Plan** in the last weeks of the previous quarter.
**Execute** with **weekly or biweekly check-ins** on KRs.
**Review**: grade OKRs, retro on what was learned.
Feed lessons into the next plan.

analogy.title: Farming seasons
analogy.story: Plant, tend, harvest, then plan the next planting based on what grew well.
analogy.breaks: Seasons are fixed by nature. Quarters are conventions, so adjust if your domain moves faster.

example.title: Q3 planning for a platform team
example.scenario: Turning lessons into the next plan.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Overcommitment, so Q3 has two objectives, not four.

example.outcome: each quarter's plan is better than the last.

check.q: Why are annual plans alone insufficient?
check.a: Assumptions expire within months; quarterly cycles allow timely course correction.

connecting-strategy-to-daily-engineering.core: Strategy reaches Monday morning through decomposition: company OKR → team OKR → epics → stories → tasks. Every ticket should trace back to a goal.

first_principles.problem: Engineers hear 'win enterprise' and don't know what to do differently. Sprint tickets feel disconnected from strategy.
derivation: Decompose **company → team OKR → epics → stories → tasks**.
Link tickets to **epics**, epics to **KRs**.
Ask of each ticket: **which goal does this serve?**
Reserve capacity for **KTLO** (keep the lights on).

analogy.title: A relay race
analogy.story: The team's goal is to win; each runner knows exactly which leg is theirs and how it contributes.
analogy.breaks: A race has one track. Engineering also needs maintenance work that doesn't map to OKRs.

example.title: 'Win enterprise' on Monday
flow: Team KR: SSO for all apps

steps.label: Meaning
steps.detail: The engineer knows why their task matters.

check.q: What does KTLO mean and why reserve capacity for it?
check.a: Keep the lights on: maintenance that doesn't map to OKRs but must still be done.
